video_title: "They Have to Print Trillions" The Next Big Print Will Trigger a 35% V-Bottom Crash
gist: Jem Carson (founder/CIO, Kai Wealth) argues five converging pressures (populism, inflation, unsustainable debt, a too-big-to-fail $300T equity market, and China) leave the US government only one exit: print money and buy strategic stocks via a sovereign wealth fund, rolled out behind a manufactured crisis. His base case is a 25-35% V-shaped equity crash in a window from after the midterms to roughly April-June 2027, best played with puts (AI names, long cyber vs. short other tech), FX vol, commodity currencies and gold, with crypto expected to rally into year-end and then suffer a sharp liquidation that becomes a buying opportunity.

themes.theme: Government as the dominant market player

insights.claim: Jem Carson argues that since 2025 the US government (administration, Treasury, Fed) has become the dominant 'player at the table' in markets, acting proactively rather than reactively, so reading its incentives now matters more than traditional macro and options-flow analysis.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Model policy reaction functions and political calendars as primary market drivers, not just macro data and dealer positioning.
insights.quote: there is a new big entrance, somebody sitting on the other side of the table, right, with a really big stack who has been really bullying the market around a bit

insights.claim: Five simultaneously accelerating structural pressures (populism, inflation, an unsustainable and accelerating national debt, an equity market too big to fail, and competition with China) are forcing aggressive US government action regardless of who is in office.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Frames policy as forced rather than discretionary, implying continued debasement-friendly policy across administrations.

insights.claim: Carson says the appointment of hedge fund managers (Treasury Secretary Bessent and Warsh) to key posts reflects that the market is now everything: controlling market direction means controlling liquidity.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Expect policymakers to actively manage equity drawdowns and engineer V-bottoms rather than let markets clear.
insights.quote: If you can control the direction of the market and you can manage that market, you are controlling liquidity. This is not conspiracy. This is reality.

insights.claim: Government stake-taking in Intel and MP Materials at all-time market highs, and Bessent's monthly buybacks of long-dated Treasuries ($3-9 billion) whenever yields exceed a level, are described as 'boiling the frog' to normalize larger-scale intervention later.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Treat current small-scale stakes and buybacks as precursors to explicit, scaled equity purchases and a long-end yield cap.
insights.quote: At all-time highs, we've been taking Intel and MP materials, all these other companies taking shares. That's never happened before outside of a crisis.

insights.claim: Carson views Hank Paulson's surprise 45-minute Bloomberg appearance, his first media interview in about four years, warning of a coming Treasury crisis and calling for a Treasury-market backstop facility, as a trial balloon coordinated with Treasury.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: A Treasury-market backstop facility is a likely policy response; watch for it as a signal that the 'big print' is starting.
insights.quote: There's zero chance in my mind that Hank Pollson Yeah. does not talk to the Treasury before he all of a sudden appears on Bloomberg

insights.claim: Carson calls Liberation Day (150% tariffs walked back almost overnight to a delay and 10-15% rates) and the spring 'end of civilization' threat quickly followed by a deal 'manufactured' crises: create vol expansion, pull in trend-following and vol-targeting shorts, then compress vol into a V-bottom rally.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Policy-induced selloffs are buying opportunities; the playbook is spike vol, flush systematic shorts, then reverse.
insights.quote: Both of those things in both cases were manufactured nonsense.

insights.claim: Carson puts combined public and private US equity value at about $300 trillion; the 20% S&P 500 rally in April-May took it from $250T to $300T, adding $50T of collateral, which he calls about 5x the tech-bubble level relative to GDP.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Equity wealth is now the main driver of liquidity and earnings, so a drawdown hits the real economy reflexively and forces policy support.
insights.quote: That is a $50 trillion increase in collateral.

insights.claim: For scale, Carson notes that all COVID-era QE was about $10 trillion and a decade of passed fiscal spending about $10 trillion, while two months of rally created $50 trillion of new collateral.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Market moves now dwarf policy flows in liquidity terms; a reversal would be a larger liquidity shock than QE ever was.

insights.claim: Market breadth is extremely poor: Carson says 60% of S&P 500 stocks are in a bear market (down 20%) with the index near all-time highs, and 45% of constituents have a negative one-year beta to the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Index-level strength masks broad weakness; concentration risk in the leaders is extreme.
insights.quote: 45% of the S&P 500 has a negative beta to the S&P 500.

insights.claim: If the bottom 94% of S&P 500 constituents went to zero, the top 6% alone would leave the index at about 4,400, its late-2023 level.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Index exposure is effectively a bet on a handful of mega caps; hedges should target the concentrated leaders.

insights.claim: Citing a Carlyle Group report, Carson says roughly 100% of S&P 500 earnings growth comes from markets going up (marked-up equity holdings and collateral-funded capex flowing back as earnings), not operational improvement.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Earnings are reflexive to prices; a 20% decline would reverse earnings growth, undermining valuation multiples built on it.
insights.quote: about 100% of earning growth is coming simply from markets going up

insights.claim: Carson cites the tech bubble as precedent: 27% earnings growth in 1999 reversed in 2000 once the bubble burst.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Market-driven earnings booms historically reverse sharply; don't extrapolate current EPS growth.

insights.claim: Carson says S&P 500 earnings growth is accelerating while cash flow growth is declining, and 90% of S&P 500 companies have negative earnings growth, a 'tale of two markets' driven by a reflexive loop.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: The gap between earnings and cash flow signals low-quality earnings; screen on cash flow, not EPS.
insights.quote: Cash flow are going falling out of bed.

themes.theme: The big print and a US sovereign wealth fund

insights.claim: Carson argues the only way out of the five pressures is for the US to print money and buy stocks, and that it will start within the next 3-6 months (and be underway within nine months), not years from now.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Position for both debasement and a policy-supported equity rebound in strategic names on a short horizon.
insights.quote: two buy stocks and what most people don't realize is that's what's coming and not coming in two years or three years or five years it's coming in the next three to six months

insights.claim: The US will buy equities through a sovereign wealth fund rather than the central bank, following Japan, where the BOJ monetized debt aggressively for 15-20 years and bought about 8% of the Nikkei.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Japan's precedent suggests a durable, policy-driven bid under favored equities.
insights.quote: Japan owns 8% of the Nikk.

insights.claim: Carson sees a US sovereign wealth fund growing to about $5 trillion within two years, eventually toward $10 trillion, compared with Norway's fund of roughly $2.6-2.7 trillion.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: A multi-trillion-dollar government buyer could re-rate the stocks it picks.
insights.quote: Can it be $5 trillion within two years? Yes.

insights.claim: A sovereign wealth fund lets the US direct investment for strategic rather than profit reasons, copying China's 10-20 years of direct state investment in solar, EVs, nuclear and infrastructure, and lets the executive branch pick winners and losers.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Favor sectors the state deems strategic (those competing with China) over pure profit-maximizers.
insights.quote: The sovereign wealth fund allows you to direct strategically investment for strategic reasons, not for profit incentives.

insights.claim: Carson says the policy will be sold as 'right-wing populism' (Trump accounts and a sovereign wealth fund holding stocks on citizens' behalf that can't be sold or spent) instead of redistribution, because handing people cash would add structural inflation.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Asset purchases rather than direct transfers mean the inflation shows up more in asset prices than in consumer demand.
insights.quote: They're going to respond with right-wing populism, which is we bought these stocks for you.

insights.claim: The end goal is negative real rates to monetize the debt, with a harder cap on long-end yields (not allowed to reach 10-20%); unlike 1968-1982, when the S&P 500 had a -40% real return as rates hit 20%, buying stocks is meant to avoid multiple and margin collapse.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Expect yield curve control on the long end plus equity support, which favors real assets and strategic equities over nominal bonds.
insights.quote: The whole game is to create negative real rates.

insights.claim: Carson warns that sustained negative real rates eventually trigger an inflationary loop (borrow at 5% to buy assets inflating at 7%, which pushes inflation to 9%, then 12%), and the US is deliberately giving up price stability.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: The long-run risk is runaway inflation; keep inflation hedges beyond the near-term trade.
insights.quote: We are purposely going to drive a lack of price stability so we can monetize the debt and we can drive growth.

insights.claim: Big new facilities need a crisis as political cover (a show of Fed independence); Carson expects facilities with very large capacity rolled out quickly in the crisis and used over the following 2.5-3 years, rather than an immediate $40 trillion print.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: The crisis is a catalyst for multi-year liquidity programs; position for a sustained reflation after the drop.
insights.quote: every new facility, every new thing has come out of major crisis

insights.claim: Carson expects no major sell-off before the midterms because the administration wants strong markets going in; the window for a manufactured crisis runs from after the midterms to about June next year, and 2028 is too late politically.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Stay long or neutral into the midterms and build downside convexity for late 2026 through mid-2027.

insights.claim: Carson's base case is a 25-35% equity decline, somewhere between Liberation Day and COVID in size, playing out as a V-shaped event over three months or less, probably one to two months.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Use short-dated convex hedges and keep cash ready to buy the V; don't position for a long bear market.
insights.quote: I've been trying to say closer to 25 35 as my base case.

insights.claim: Possible triggers he lists: a Treasury/bond crisis (as Paulson warned), an inflation shock from Strait of Hormuz disruption, or an AI-related cyber or digital breakdown that crashes an already concentrated market.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Watch long-end yields, oil and AI/cyber incidents as candidate catalysts.

insights.claim: A wave of 2021-era 0% refinancing with 5-7 year duration comes due in 2026-2027, adding to long-end pressure alongside sovereign selling and gold buying; Carson says the government doesn't mind rising yields because they justify a backstop facility.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Expect continued upward pressure on long yields until a backstop or yield cap is announced.
insights.quote: everybody refinanced in 2021.

insights.claim: If the plan hasn't started by about April-June next year, Carson doesn't think it will be executed in this form; the government might instead buy stocks and print at all-time highs without a crisis, at some cost to perception.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: A clear expiry date for the thesis; reassess hedges if nothing happens by mid-2027.

insights.claim: Carson says the short, sharp crisis scenario is a fringe outcome and a big call, but much more likely than markets are pricing; risks to the plan include China, AI oligarchs, loss of control in a crisis, and damage to the dollar's privilege.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Underpriced tail risk favors buying cheap convexity over making directional bets.
insights.quote: a short-term like crisis like this with these types of outcome, it's a it's a fringe outcome

insights.claim: Carson argues the Venezuela and Iran interventions were about stopping China's yuan-for-oil trade; the worst case still achieved in Iran is US control of the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East oil flows, which backs the dollar's reserve status.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Read US Middle East policy as dollar defense; oil-flow control lets the US debase with no alternative reserve currency available.
insights.quote: The reason why we're in Iran is the same reason we went into Venezuela. China started trading in yuan for oil.

insights.claim: Carson says the Houthis bombed Saudi pipelines rerouting oil around Hormuz and then took control of the strait, but the US made a deal with the Houthis so US ships pass freely, leaving the US in control of Middle East oil flows.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: An energy chokepoint under US influence supports dollar leverage and US energy and commodity positioning.
insights.quote: All oil coming out of the Middle East is controlled by the UNI United States.

insights.claim: Carson argues reserve currency status rests on power, not popularity, so actions that look like they undermine the dollar are a deliberate 'shoot the moon' strategy to escape built-up pressures.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Don't bet on near-term loss of the dollar's reserve status, but expect currency debasement against hard assets.

themes.theme: Positioning: inflation winners, hedges, FX and gold

insights.claim: About 25% of the S&P 500 sees profit margins expand as inflation and rates rise: negative working capital businesses, middlemen and brokers (real estate, financial), banks, telecom, railroads and asset managers. The other 75% see margins contract.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Overweight inflation-margin beneficiaries and strategic or structural inflation hedges for the next 5-10 years.
insights.quote: anybody who's taking volumes are going to expand, but their costs will not expand

insights.claim: Avoid businesses that depend on the lower-end consumer or are cost-constrained, such as McDonald's, because inflation will squeeze their margins.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Underweight or short low-end consumer names with tight margins.

insights.claim: Gold will do well, as it did after the 1970s move off gold and Arthur Burns' negative real rates (the best-performing asset for 12-15 years, but also the most volatile); Carson favors gold calls and buying the current dip after advising a pause during early-year silver mania.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Accumulate gold, ideally via calls, on pullbacks ahead of debasement.
insights.quote: you want to own calls in gold

insights.claim: For the crash, Carson recommends defined-risk equity puts, focused on AI names more than just the S&P 500, or a long cyber vs. short other tech pair as a lower-risk relative-value expression.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Buy puts on concentrated AI leaders; consider long cyber / short broad tech.
insights.quote: I think uh you know cyber names are interesting uh relative to other tech names

insights.claim: Carson thinks FX volatility is dramatically underpriced given the global currency implications, and prefers holding cash in commodity-backed or non-USD currencies: Swiss franc, Norwegian krone, Australian and Canadian dollars.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Buy FX vol; hold dry powder in CHF, NOK, AUD and CAD rather than USD.
insights.quote: I do think that FXVA is dramatically underpriced

themes.theme: Crypto: two buyer bases and a rug-pull risk

insights.claim: Crypto has two buyer bases: institutions treating it as a debasement-trade store of value alongside gold, and tech investors treating it as transformative technology. It is most bullish when both tech and debasement trades work, as now.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Track tech-equity momentum as a crypto driver; a tech rollover hits crypto even in a debasement regime.
insights.quote: is crypto like gold or is it like tech >> and the answer is yes.

insights.claim: Carson expects crypto to do well into the midterms and a top around December-January, then a rug pull early next year as tech rolls over, with a liquidation that becomes one of the best buying opportunities ahead of the debasement trade.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Take profits or hedge crypto into year-end; plan to buy the early-2027 drawdown.
insights.quote: right at that moment rug pull early next year in the market

insights.claim: Carson thinks crypto, possibly including stakes in companies like Strategy (about 850,000 BTC, per the host), will likely be part of the administration's efforts over the next 2-3 years, partly to keep a retail army buying stocks.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Bitcoin-linked equities could benefit from government-driven buying.

insights.claim: Carson argues crypto's value rests on belief, especially among millennials hurt by 40 years of supply-side economics, who are now gaining political dominance. Long term, though, those in power won't let anti-power money become the standard; he sees a roughly 20-year runway.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Bullish over multiple years on demographic flows, with long-term regulatory or sovereign risk to crypto as a currency.
insights.quote: those in power by definition do not want crypto to grow and to become the standard because it undermines power at large

insights.claim: The stablecoin legislation (Genius Act) steers crypto flows to support the dollar; Carson says it has been 'incredibly helpful and successful for power'.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth adds structural demand for Treasuries and the dollar.

themes.theme: AI regulatory capture as a crisis vector

insights.claim: Carson, flagging it as very speculative, reads the sudden joint call from rival AI leaders (Dario Amodei, Altman, Musk) to slow AI development, plus Anthropic hiring Accenture to audit safety, as a defensive move against looming government ownership and regulatory capture.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Government ownership stakes in AI leaders are a real policy risk for AI equity valuations.
insights.quote: to me this is very clearly about regulatory capture.

insights.claim: With Bernie Sanders floating 50% government ownership of AI and Palantir's Karp saying AI leaders are poor stewards and the US should have control, Carson sees an AI-related crisis such as a cyberattack as a possible pretext for government control and a market crash in already concentrated AI names.
insights.speaker: Jem Carson
insights.so_what: Watch for AI or cyber incidents; puts on AI mega caps hedge both crash and nationalization risk.
